SIMPLE CASES.
[126.
Hence
$$\begin{aligned}
& F=\frac{b^{2}}{8} \frac{(A-B)^{2}}{(b-a)^{2}}=\frac{e_{1}^{2}}{8 a^{2}} \\
& T=\frac{b^{2}(A-B)^{2}}{16 \pi a}(b-a)^{2}
\end{aligned}$$
If a spherical soap bubble is electrified to a potential $A$, then,
if its radius is $u$, the charge will be $A u$, and the surface-density
will be
$$\sigma=\frac{1}{4 \pi} \frac{A}{a} .$$
The resultant intensity just outside the surface will be $4 \pi \sigma$,
and inside the bubble it is zero, so that by Art. 79 the electric
force on unit of area of the surface will be $2 \pi \sigma^{2}$, acting outwards.
Hence the electrification will diminish the pressure of the air
within the bubble by $2 \pi \sigma^{2}$, or
$$\frac{1}{8 \pi} \frac{A^{2}}{a^{2}} .$$
But it may be shewn that if $T_{0}$ is the tension which the liquid
film exerts across a line of unit length, then the pressure from
within required to keep the bubble from collapsing is $2 T_{0}^{\prime} / a_{\text {. }}$ If
the electric force is just sufficient to keep the bubble in equi-
librium when the air within and without is at the same pressure,
$$A^{2}=16 \pi \alpha T_{0} .$$

Two Infinite Coaxal Cylindric Surfaces.
126.] Let the radius of the outer surface of a conducting
cylinder be $a$, and let the radius of an inner surface of a hollow
cylinder, having the same axis with the first, be $b$. Let their
potentials be $A$ and $B$ respectively. Then, since the potential $V$
is in this case a function only of $r$, the distance from the axis,
Laplace's equation becomes
$$\frac{d^{2} V}{d r^{2}}+\frac{1}{r} \frac{d V}{d r}=0,$$
whence
$$V=C_{1}+C_{2} \log r .$$
Since $V=A$ when $r=a$, and $V=b$ when $r=b$,
$$V=\frac{A \log \frac{b}{r}+B \log \frac{r}{a}}{\log \frac{b}{a}}$$

\section*{Two Infinite Coaxal Cylindric Surfaces.}

126.] Let the radius of the outer surface of a conducting
 cylinder be $a$, and let the radius of an inner surface of a hollow
 cylinder, having the same axis with the first, be $b$. Let their
 potentials be $A$ and $B$ respectively. Then, since the potential $V$
 is in this case a function only of $r$, the distance from the axis,
 Laplace's equation becomes

$$\frac{d^{2} V}{d r^{2}}+\frac{1}{r} \frac{d V}{d r}=0,$$

$$V=C_{1}+C_{2} \log r .$$


Since $V=A$ when $r=a$, and $V=b$ when $r=b$,

$$V=\frac{A \log \frac{b}{r}+B \log \frac{r}{a}}{\log \frac{b}{a}}$$
